section.title: Timothy's Encouraging Report
section.sectionRationale: Torn from them and unable to return, Paul sent Timothy to strengthen the young church, fearing the tempter had shaken their faith under persecution. Timothy's report of their steadfast faith and love brings Paul from anxiety to overflowing thanksgiving, ending in a prayer that God would establish their hearts blameless at the coming of the Lord.
section.thesis: Paul's deep love for a suffering church, his sending of Timothy, and his relief at their standing firm show that Christian ministry is bound up with affection, prayer, and dependence on God, who alone strengthens hearts and keeps His people blameless until Christ comes.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Paul's longing and thwarted attempts to return; the sending of Timothy amid fear for their faith; and Timothy's good report, Paul's overflowing thanks, and his prayer for their establishment before Christ.

units.label: Longing to return
units.note: torn away, yet bound in heart

verses.text: Brothers, although we were torn away from you for a short time (in person, not in heart), our desire to see you face to face was even more intense.
For we wanted to come to you, indeed I, Paul, tried again and again, but {{satanas|Satan}} obstructed us.
After all, who is our hope, our joy, our crown of {{kauchesis|boasting}}, if it is not you yourselves in the presence of our Lord Jesus at His {{parousia|coming}}?
You are indeed our glory and our joy.

units.label: Sending Timothy
units.note: to strengthen a faith under trial

verses.text: So when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left on our own in Athens.
We sent Timothy, our brother and fellow worker for God in the gospel of Christ, to {{sterizo|strengthen}} and encourage you in your {{pistis|faith}},
so that none of you would be shaken by these trials. For you know that we are destined for this.
Indeed, when we were with you, we kept warning you that we would suffer persecution; and as you know, it has come to pass.
For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the {{peirazo|tempter}} had somehow tempted you and that our labor might have been in vain.

units.label: The good report and Paul's prayer
units.note: relief, thanksgiving, and a plea for blameless hearts

verses.text: But just now, Timothy has returned from his visit with the good news about your faith, your {{agape|love}}, and the fond memories you have preserved, longing to see us just as we long to see you.
For this reason, brothers, in all our {{thlipsis|distress}} and persecution, we have been reassured about you, because of your faith.
For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord.
How can we adequately thank God for you in return for our great joy over you in His presence?
Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith.
Now may our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you.
And may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else, just as our love for you overflows,
so that He may establish your hearts in blamelessness and {{hagiosyne|holiness}} before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His {{hagioi|saints}}. Amen.

satanas.gloss: Satan, the adversary, the personal enemy of God and His people. Paul says Satan obstructed his repeated attempts to return to Thessalonica. The word names a real opponent behind the frustrations of ministry, though Paul is confident that even Satan cannot finally thwart God's purpose for the church.

kauchesis.gloss: Boasting, the act of glorying or exulting in something. Paul calls the Thessalonians his crown of boasting in the presence of the Lord at His coming. His glorying is not in himself but in the fruit of the gospel; the converts he loves are his joy and reward before Christ.

parousia.gloss: Coming, arrival, or presence, used for the return of the Lord Jesus. Paul looks ahead to Christ's parousia, when the Thessalonians will be his joy and crown. The word becomes a key term across the letter for the second coming and frames Paul's hopes, prayers, and warnings.

sterizo.gloss: To strengthen, establish, or make firm. Timothy was sent to strengthen the Thessalonians in their faith so they would not be shaken. The same idea returns in the closing prayer that God would establish their hearts. Believers are steadied not by their own grip but by God's strengthening work.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust in God that holds firm under pressure. Their faith is Paul's central concern throughout this section: he fears for it, sends Timothy to bolster it, rejoices at its steadfastness, and prays to supply what is lacking in it. Faith that stands under trial is the mark of a genuine work of God.

peirazo.gloss: To tempt or test. Paul names the tempter, the one who tempts, his fear being that Satan had lured the young believers away under the pressure of persecution. The word underlines the spiritual danger of trials: suffering can be an occasion the enemy uses to try to shake faith.

agape.gloss: Self-giving love. Timothy reports their faith and their love, and Paul prays the Lord will make their love increase and overflow toward one another and toward all. Love is both evidence of their standing in Christ and the very thing Paul asks God to enlarge in them.

thlipsis.gloss: Affliction, distress, pressure. Paul speaks of his own distress and persecution, in the midst of which the good news of their faith brings him fresh life. The word describes the crushing pressure both he and the church endure, the very setting in which their faith is proved genuine.

hagiosyne.gloss: Holiness, the quality of being set apart and morally pure. Paul prays that God would establish their hearts in blamelessness and holiness before Him at Christ's coming. Holiness here is the goal of God's strengthening work, a heart made fit to stand before God on the last day.

hagioi.gloss: Holy ones or saints. Paul looks to the coming of the Lord Jesus with all His saints. The term may include angels, glorified believers, or both, who accompany Christ at His return. It sets the closing prayer within the grand scene of the Lord's appearing in glory.

basic.context: Paul had been forced to leave Thessalonica and could not get back, though he tried repeatedly. Worried sick that persecution might have crushed their new faith, he sent Timothy to check on them and strengthen them. When Timothy returned with good news that they were standing firm, Paul was flooded with relief and thanks, and he closes with a heartfelt prayer for them.
basic.hermeneutics: This is deeply personal, showing the affection and anxiety of a real pastor for a real church. We read it as a window into godly ministry: love, prayer, and dependence on God. The closing prayer, that God would make them holy and blameless at Christ's coming, states what God does for all His people.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul says satanas, Satan, blocked his return, yet the Thessalonians are his crown of kauchesis, boasting, at Christ's parousia, coming. He sent Timothy to sterizo, strengthen, their pistis, faith, fearing the peirazo, tempter. Timothy's report of their faith and agape, love, brings relief in Paul's thlipsis, distress. He prays God would establish them in hagiosyne, holiness, when the Lord comes with all His hagioi, saints.
basic.typology: Paul's longing for God to direct his way and to establish their hearts echoes the Old Testament hope that God would gather and keep His people. The Lord coming with all His holy ones takes up prophetic pictures of God arriving in glory with His hosts.
basic.christ: The whole passage looks to the coming of the Lord Jesus, when believers will be Paul's joy and crown and will be presented holy and blameless. Christ is the one in whom they stand firm, and He comes with all His saints in glory.
basic.god: God is the Father to whom Paul gives thanks and prays, the one who strengthens faith, causes love to overflow, and establishes hearts in holiness. Salvation and perseverance are His work; Paul's confidence for the church rests on what God will do, not merely on their effort.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 1 shows the same confidence that God will complete the good work He began. First Thessalonians 5 repeats the prayer that God would keep them blameless at Christ's coming. And Jude closes with praise to the God who keeps believers from stumbling.
basic.oneStory: God gathers a people and keeps them to the end. Here that keeping work is seen up close: a suffering church steadied through Timothy, sustained by prayer, and entrusted to the God who will establish their hearts blameless when the Lord Jesus comes with all His saints.

context.literary:
The passage begins with the second half of chapter 2 and runs through chapter 3, and the chapter break hides the fact that it is one story told in three scenes. In 2:17 to 20 Paul describes his longing and the obstacle that stopped him. In 3:1 to 5 he tells how he sent Timothy in his place. In 3:6 to 13 Timothy comes back and the story resolves in relief, thanksgiving, and prayer. The scenes are linked by repeated phrases: 'could bear it no longer' appears in 3:1 and again, almost word for word, in 3:5, a deliberate echo that frames the decision to send Timothy.

There is also a shape in the way the 'coming' of Christ frames the whole section. It appears in 2:19, when the church is Paul's crown at the Lord's coming, and again in 3:13, when Paul prays that they will be blameless at that same coming. Between those two mentions, everything that happens on earth, the obstacles, the anxiety, the reports, and the prayers, is measured against that day. The passage ends with a prayer in two parts, first for the way to open for Paul, 3:11, and then for the church to grow, 3:12 and 13. These prayers also serve as a hinge: they close the personal first half of the letter, and the words 'holiness' and 'coming' in verse 13 open the instruction of chapters 4 and 5.
context.historical:
Paul's anxiety makes sense once the timeline is clear. Luke tells us that after the riot in Thessalonica the believers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where the pursuit followed them and Paul was sent on toward the coast, Acts 17:10 to 15. He reached Athens alone, Acts 17:14 to 16, and asked Silas and Timothy to come quickly. Athens was a place of intellectual debate and of idols everywhere he looked, and Paul was without his team. From there, according to this letter, he sent Timothy back to Thessalonica, deciding to remain alone, 3:1 and 2. The reunion happened in Corinth, where Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, Acts 18:1 and 5, and this letter was written soon after, probably in AD 50 or 51.

The word that Paul had warned them of persecution in advance, 3:4, fits the sense that a convert in a Greek city would expect to be cut off from family, trade guilds, and civic festivals, all of which carried pagan worship. Timothy was a young colleague from Lystra with a Jewish mother and a Greek father, Acts 16:1 to 3, and was trusted by Paul as a stand-in, as in Philippians 2:19 to 22 and 1 Corinthians 4:17. Sending a delegate was an accepted way of keeping a relationship in an age of slow letters and long journeys.
context.canonical:
The picture of Paul as a pastor anxious for a church from a distance is found throughout his letters. He speaks of the daily pressure of his concern for all the churches in 2 Corinthians 11:28, of being in labour again until Christ is formed in the Galatians, Galatians 4:19, and of the worry that led him to send Titus to Corinth, 2 Corinthians 2:12 and 13 and 7:5 to 7. The relief he expresses in 3:6 to 8 is the same relief he describes when Titus arrived with good news.

The theme of stable faith under pressure echoes Jesus' parable of the soil in which some seed springs up quickly and then withers when trouble comes, Mark 4:16 and 17. Paul's fear that the tempter had been at work recalls the temptation narratives, Matthew 4:3, where the same title is used, and Peter's later warning that the devil prowls about, 1 Peter 5:8 and 9.

The prayer of verses 12 and 13 is a pattern that is repeated across the New Testament. Compare Philippians 1:9 to 11, 1 Thessalonians 5:23, and Jude 24, each of which asks God to keep His people blameless until the end. The coming of the Lord with His holy ones connects the passage with Zechariah 14:5 and with Jesus' own words in Matthew 25:31. Paul is placing a young church in the sweep of the whole biblical hope.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Paul wants the church to feel what he feels, which is both his love for them and his dependence on their steadfastness, and to understand that his earlier absence was not abandonment. He tells the story of his anxiety and Timothy's mission so they will see that he has been thinking of them every day. He also wants them to see what he is really worried about. It is not whether they like him, but whether their faith will survive the trials he warned them of. He brings the issue of suffering into the open and says plainly that it is part of Christian life, and so he moves from comfort to teaching. The closing prayer is not only an expression of affection. It is a statement of what he believes God will do and what he hopes they will become, and by praying aloud for them in the letter he gives them the words to pray for each other and the assurance that their growth is not left to their own strength.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Almost everything here is narrative and personal. Paul says what he felt, what he tried, whom he sent, and what he prayed. That should keep us from turning it into a rulebook, as though every pastor must send a delegate whenever a church is in trouble, or must feel exactly this anguish. What is lasting is the way the story shows love in action: concern put into effort, prayers that name particular people, and a readiness to give up one's own comfort for the sake of others, as Paul was willing to be left alone in Athens. The one statement that is plainly general is 'we are destined for this,' verse 3, which says that trial is part of ordinary Christian life. It describes the pattern the church should expect, not a punishment to be searched out. The prayer in verses 12 and 13 is not a command but a model: Christians may pray for one another's love and holiness in the same way.

debates.question: Who are the 'saints' who come with the Lord Jesus in verse 13?

views.label: Angels
views.case: The Old Testament picture of the LORD coming 'with all the holy ones,' Zechariah 14:5, Deuteronomy 33:2, and Jesus' words about the Son of Man coming with all His angels, Matthew 25:31 and Mark 8:38, lead many readers to see angelic hosts here. 2 Thessalonians 1:7 also speaks of the Lord Jesus appearing with His mighty angels.

views.label: Believers who have died and will return with Christ
views.case: The word is regularly used of believers, and the letter itself says that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him, 4:14. This view takes verse 13 as a preview of that teaching, and notes that the prayer is about the Thessalonians' own holiness being found complete when they meet all their fellow believers.

views.label: Both together
views.case: A third approach observes that the phrase could cover angels and redeemed people together, as in Colossians 3:4, where believers appear with Christ in glory, and Revelation 19:14, where the armies of heaven follow Him.

debates.bearing: Whichever group is meant, the verse's weight falls on the Thessalonians standing blameless before their God and Father in that company. The prayer is about their readiness, and it should not be used as a map of the end times.

debates.question: What does it mean that Satan 'obstructed' Paul, when Paul also prays that God will direct his way?

views.label: Satan used specific, human circumstances
views.case: Some point to Acts 17:9, where Jason and the others were made to post security, and suggest the agreement kept Paul out of the city. The hindrance was real and traceable, yet Paul reads it as the work of the adversary and not mere bad luck.

views.label: God permits Satan's opposition for His own purposes
views.case: Others note that Scripture portrays Satan as limited, acting only by permission, Job 1:12 and 2:6, Luke 22:31, and 2 Corinthians 12:7 to 10. Paul sees the delay as an attack but prays to God who directs, verse 11, trusting that God remains in control.

views.label: Paul sees the conflict as spiritual warfare, not a puzzle of providence
views.case: A third view stresses that Paul does not explain how the two forces relate and does not try to. He simply names the opposition honestly and prays to God, whose will cannot finally be defeated.

debates.bearing: The passage lets Paul hold both thoughts at once without resolving them: the adversary is real, and the Father and the Son are the ones who steer. For a believer whose plans have been blocked, it gives permission to call the obstacle what it is and still pray for the way to open.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 17 holds one of the most striking words in the passage. When Paul says he was 'torn away' from them, the verb is aporphanizo, which comes from the word for an orphan. Literally Paul says that he was 'orphaned' from the Thessalonians. It is the language of a parent, not of a missionary, and it adds to the image of the family in the previous chapter. The separation is described in words of bereavement, though Paul quickly qualifies it: 'in person, not in heart.'

In verse 18 the word 'obstructed' is the verb enkopto, which means to hinder or to cut in on. It was used of someone who blocks the way. Paul uses it elsewhere of being hindered from visiting Rome, Romans 15:22. 'Again and again' translates a phrase that literally means 'once and twice,' an idiom for more than once, found also in Philippians 4:16.

In 3:3 the verb 'shaken' is sainesthai, a rare word that can carry the sense of being disturbed or drawn aside. The point is that trials could knock them off course. The word for 'destined' is keimetha, from keimai, 'to be placed', so that Paul says suffering is a thing we are 'laid down for,' set in the order of things by God and not an accident.

Verse 6 says Timothy 'brought good news,' using euangelizomai, the verb that is elsewhere used for announcing the gospel. Here it carries ordinary news, and the effect is that the report of their steadfastness is almost a second gospel to him. In verse 8 'standing firm' translates a verb, stēkō, built from the perfect of 'to stand', so that it suggests having taken a stand and remaining there.

Verse 10 has two powerful words. 'Most earnestly' is hyperekperissou, a triple compound that piles up intensity, meaning something like 'beyond all measure and more.' 'Supply' is katartizo, a verb for mending or equipping, used of fishermen mending their nets, Mark 1:19. Paul wants to fix what is unfinished in their faith, not criticise it.

In verse 11 the verb 'direct' is singular, even though its subjects are 'our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus.' Two persons are named, and a single verb is used, a grammatical sign of the unity with which Paul prays. Verse 12 combines two verbs of growth, pleonazo and perisseuo, 'increase' and 'overflow'. The first suggests becoming more; the second suggests spilling over the edges.

typology.type: The people of God as a crown, 1 Thessalonians 2:19
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 62:3 tells Israel that she will be a crown of splendour in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the hand of her God. Paul borrows the picture and turns it: the Thessalonians are his crown, but only in the presence of the Lord at His coming. In Christ the believers are the reward and joy of the apostle and also the 'glory' that the Lord shares with them. The type falls short because Isaiah's crown is the nation held by God; Paul's crown is a church from every nation, and Philippians 4:1 uses the same phrase for another church.

typology.type: The adversary who can only act within limits, 1 Thessalonians 2:18
typology.fulfillment: The accuser stands before the LORD in Zechariah 3:1 and 2 and is rebuked, and in Job he can act only when and as far as God allows, Job 1:12. Paul's experience matches that pattern. Satan hinders, but he does not prevail. In Christ the correspondence reaches its centre: Jesus saw Satan fall from heaven, Luke 10:18, and disarmed the powers by the cross, Colossians 2:15. The type falls short because the Old Testament accuser still had access to God's court; the cross has decisively answered the accusation, Revelation 12:10 and 11.

typology.type: The LORD coming with His holy ones, 1 Thessalonians 3:13
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah 14:5 closes with the LORD my God coming, and all the holy ones with Him, and Deuteronomy 33:2 speaks of God coming from Sinai with ten thousand holy ones. Paul takes the picture and gives it a name: 'our Lord Jesus.' In Christ the divine arrival is both the Lord God and the risen Son, as Jesus Himself said in Matthew 25:31. The type falls short because the prophets spoke of a day of conflict on a mountain outside Jerusalem; the New Testament speaks of the same coming but as the victory of the Son, who gathers the whole church.

typology.type: The heart established in love, 1 Thessalonians 3:12 and 13
typology.fulfillment: Moses promised that the LORD would circumcise the hearts of His people so they could love Him, Deuteronomy 30:6, and Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 promised a new heart and a Spirit within. Paul prays for exactly this to grow and overflow in the Thessalonians. In Christ the promise becomes a gift: God's love is poured into believers' hearts by the Spirit, Romans 5:5, and the new commandment is to love as He loved, John 13:34. The type falls short because the old covenant could only point to what the heart needed; the new one carries it out.

study.christ:
This passage lets the reader see how thoroughly the Lord Jesus is woven into Paul's thinking, even in a section about travel plans and anxiety. His name appears at the beginning of the section, 2:19, in the middle, 3:2 and 3:8, and at the end, 3:11 and 13. He is the one before whom Paul stands at the last day, the one in whom the Thessalonians must stand firm, and one of two persons who may direct the way to them.

The prayer of verse 11 is remarkable. Paul writes 'may our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way,' with a single verb for both. He does not suggest that Jesus is a lesser helper. He prays to Jesus in the same breath and with the same grammar as to the Father. Early readers recognised this as a sign of the Son's divinity. The same pairing recurs in 2 Thessalonians 2:16 and 17, where 'our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, and God our Father' comfort and strengthen together.

The Lord is also the one who causes love to grow. Verse 12 says 'may the Lord cause you to increase and overflow.' In Paul's usage 'the Lord' normally means Jesus, and this makes the work of forming a loving community the Lord's own. It echoes His promise that the world would know His disciples by their love, John 13:35. The Lord Jesus is not only an example for love but the source of it.

The final element is the Lord's coming. Verse 13 describes it as the moment at which believers will stand 'before our God and Father,' and the whole prayer is aimed at it. The cross is not mentioned in this passage, but it is the reason for the confidence. Because Christ has already been raised and has promised to return, Paul can ask for blamelessness as something God will in fact do. Colossians 1:22 says the aim of the cross was to present believers holy and blameless before God, and Jude 24 says it will be done by the one who is able to keep them from falling.

We should not make the passage say more than it does. It does not describe the manner of the Lord's coming, which is taken up in chapter 4. Its contribution is to show how a pastor's prayer for ordinary people, their love and their holiness, finds its meaning in the coming of Christ.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who is addressed as Father and who acts as Father. The phrase 'our God and Father' appears twice in the prayer, verses 11 and 13, and marks the relationship in which everything else is held. Paul does not pray to a distant ruler but to a Father who has the standing to direct journeys and the power to shape hearts.

The passage also shows what God does in the lives of believers, and how it differs from what Paul and Timothy could do. Timothy can strengthen and encourage, 3:2, and Paul can pray and visit, but only God can establish hearts. Verse 13 uses the verb 'establish' for something that is God's to do: to make firm, to confirm in blamelessness and holiness. Human ministry is real, and it is also a means by which God works. This gives the church both a task and a rest. It must send, visit, and pray, and yet the outcome rests with the one who keeps.

Third, the passage holds together God's rule and the reality of opposition. Satan really obstructed Paul, and the Thessalonians really suffered. Yet Paul does not pray as though the two sides were equal. His prayer is addressed to the God who is able to direct his way, and the end of the passage looks to a day when God will present His people blameless. The adversary operates inside a story that God is writing.

Fourth, God is the giver of love. Verse 12 prays that the Lord will cause love to overflow 'for one another and for everyone else.' Love is not only a response to God's love; it is something He works in people, and it is meant to spill beyond the borders of the church. The God of the passage is a generous God whose character is reproduced in His people.

For worship, the passage invites thankfulness over answered concern, as in verse 9, where Paul asks how he could ever thank God enough. It also invites persistent prayer, since Paul prays 'night and day,' and it invites trust that the God who began a work will complete it, as Philippians 1:6 says.

crossReferences.note: Luke's account of Paul's flight from Thessalonica to Berea and then to Athens. It supplies the background to 'torn away' and 'left on our own in Athens,' and shows how quickly the missionaries were scattered.

Silas and Timothy arrive in Corinth from Macedonia, and Paul is 'devoted to the word.' This is likely the moment Timothy returned with the good news of 3:6, and it explains why the letter's joy is so fresh.

Paul says he has no one like Timothy, who genuinely cares for others' welfare and has served with him like a son with a father. It helps us see why Paul trusted him with the delicate task of strengthening the church.

Paul calls the Philippians his joy and crown, the same pair of words as in 1 Thessalonians 2:19 and 20. The repetition shows that the language is a settled way of speaking of converts as the pastor's reward before Christ.

Seed on rocky ground springs up with joy but withers when trouble comes. Paul's fear in 3:5 that the tempter had done his work is this parable lived out by a pastor who has seen the seed spring up and cannot bear to learn it has withered.

Paul describes the same cycle in another city: conflicts without and fears within, comfort arriving through the coming of Titus with a good report. It confirms that his relief in 3:6 to 8 is typical of how he lived with churches.

The prophet sees the LORD coming with all the holy ones. This is the likely source of 'at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints,' and it shows Paul identifying Jesus with the LORD of the Old Testament.

Paul prays again that God will sanctify them completely and keep them blameless at the coming of the Lord, and adds that the one who calls is faithful and will do it. It answers the prayer of 3:13 with a promise.

Paul is confident that the one who began a good work will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. It shares the logic of 3:13: God finishes what He starts, and the finishing is aimed at the same day.

The closing doxology praises the one who is able to keep believers from stumbling and to present them without fault before His glory. It is the same confidence that stands behind 'blamelessness and holiness before our God and Father.'

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is of a God who gathers a people and then keeps them. In Genesis He calls Abraham and promises to bless him; in Exodus He brings the people through the sea and then through the desert; in the prophets He promises to establish them, and at last through the Spirit to write His law on their hearts. At each stage there is an adversary who tries to hinder, from the serpent of Genesis 3 to the tempter who came to Jesus in the wilderness. This passage shows one small, human episode of the same long conflict. A tempter threatens a church, a pastor worries, a delegate goes and returns, and the prayer goes up.

What it adds to the story is the picture of how God keeps His people in practice. He uses messengers, prayers, and reports, and He uses the love that believers have for each other. Paul's tears and Timothy's journey are not outside God's plan. They are the way the plan reaches Thessalonica.

The passage also looks to the end of the story. The coming of the Lord with all His holy ones is the goal toward which every part of the Bible moves, and the aim of the prayer is that the Thessalonians will be found ready. In the new creation the separations that caused Paul pain will be over. Revelation 21:3 promises that God will dwell with His people, and the long absence Paul felt, in which he wanted to see them face to face, will give way to a meeting where no one is torn away, and where love overflows without the trials that now test it.

sermon.why: No sermon on this specific movement, 1 Thessalonians 2:17 to 3:13, from a trusted expositor was verified by web search during this session.

quiz.q: Why did Paul send Timothy to the Thessalonians?

options.text: To strengthen and encourage their faith so they would not be shaken by trials.
options.note: Verses 2-3 give this as the reason for sending Timothy.

options.text: To collect money from the church.
options.note: Paul's concern was their faith, not funds; he refused to burden them.

options.text: To take charge and replace their leaders.
options.note: Timothy came to strengthen them in faith, not to take over.

options.text: To rebuke them for abandoning the gospel.
options.note: Paul feared for them but found they were standing firm, and he rejoiced.

quiz.q: What news did Timothy bring back that so encouraged Paul?

options.text: That the Thessalonians were standing firm in faith and love.
options.note: Verses 6-8 report their faith and love and their standing firm.

options.text: That the persecution had completely stopped.
options.note: The good news was their steadfast faith, not the end of persecution.

options.text: That the church had grown very wealthy.
options.note: Timothy reported their faith and love, not their prosperity.

options.text: That they had given up under pressure.
options.note: The opposite: they stood firm, which brought Paul relief and joy.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray God will do for the Thessalonians at the end of this section?

options.text: Establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord.
options.note: Verse 13 is this prayer for blamelessness at Christ's coming.

options.text: Make them wealthy and comfortable.
options.note: His prayer is for holiness and love, not comfort or wealth.

options.text: Remove every trial from their lives at once.
options.note: He prays for their establishment in holiness, not the removal of all trials.

options.text: Leave them to manage on their own.
options.note: He entrusts them to God, who will keep and establish them.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the Thessalonians in relation to Christ's coming?

options.text: As his hope, joy, and crown of boasting before the Lord at His coming.
options.note: Verses 19-20 call them his hope, joy, and crown at Christ's coming.

options.text: As a burden he is glad to be free of.
options.note: Far from a burden, they are his joy and crown.

options.text: As people he barely remembers.
options.note: He longs intensely to see them and treasures them deeply.

options.text: As rivals for his ministry reputation.
options.note: They are his glory and joy, the fruit he will present to the Lord.

quiz.q: What did Paul fear had happened to the young church under persecution?

options.text: That the tempter had shaken their faith and his labor had been in vain.
options.note: Verse 5 names this fear about the tempter and their faith.

options.text: That they had become too proud of their success.
options.note: His fear was for their faith under pressure, not pride.

options.text: That they had grown bored with the gospel.
options.note: The concern was the tempter exploiting persecution to shake their faith.

options.text: That they had forgotten his name.
options.note: His fear was for the survival of their faith, not his reputation.

questions: Paul was torn between churches yet remained bound to them in heart. Who are the people God has given you to love and pray for even when you cannot be with them?
Paul feared the tempter would use suffering to shake the young believers. How has trial tested your faith, and what has helped you stand firm in the Lord?
Timothy's report brought Paul from anxiety to overflowing thanks. Whose faithfulness has recently encouraged you, and have you told them or thanked God for them?
Paul prayed that their love would increase and overflow toward everyone. Whom is God calling you to love more generously, including those beyond your own circle?
The closing prayer rests everything on God establishing their hearts blameless at Christ's coming. How does it steady you to know that your final holiness is God's work and promise?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote records variants describing Timothy as God's fellow worker or as a minister of God, reflecting different manuscript readings.
The saints who come with the Lord may refer to angels, to glorified believers, or to both; the Greek term simply means holy ones.
